description: How common are armed conflict and peace between and within countries? How is this changing over time? Explore research and data on war and peace.
title: War and Peace
image: https://ourworldindata.org/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/qLq-8BTgXU8yG0N6HnOy8g/aa942158-857b-4a7a-76b1-596cc88e3f00/public
---

Since 1800, more than [37 million people](https://ourworldindata.org/war-and-peace?insight=some-conflicts-are-much-much-deadlier-than-most#key-insights) worldwide have died while actively fighting in wars.

The number would be much higher still if it also considered the civilians who died due to the fighting, the increased number of deaths from hunger and disease resulting from these conflicts, and the deaths in smaller conflicts that are not considered wars.[1](#note-1)

Wars are also terrible in many other ways: they make people’s lives insecure, lower their living standards, destroy the environment, and, if fought between countries armed with [nuclear weapons](https://ourworldindata.org/nuclear-weapons), can be an existential threat to humanity.

Looking at the news alone, it can be difficult to understand whether more or less people are dying as a result of war than in the past. One has to rely on statistics that are carefully collected so that they can be compared over time.

While every war is a tragedy, the data suggests that [fewer people died](https://ourworldindata.org/war-and-peace?insight=conflict-deaths-have-declined-it-is-on-us-that-this-trend-continues#key-insights) in conflicts in recent decades than in most of the 20th century. Countries have also built more peaceful relations [between](https://ourworldindata.org/war-and-peace?insight=relationships-between-countries-have-become-more-peaceful#key-insights) and [within](https://ourworldindata.org/democracy) them.

How many wars are avoided, and whether the trend of fewer deaths in them continues, is up to our own actions. Conflict deaths recently increased in the Middle East, Africa, and Europe, stressing that the future of these trends is uncertain.

On this page, you can find data, visualizations, and writing on how common war and peace are between and within countries, and how this has changed over time.

#### Related topics

* [Military Personnel and Spending](https://ourworldindata.org/military-personnel-spending)
* [Nuclear Weapons](https://ourworldindata.org/nuclear-weapons)
* [Terrorism](https://ourworldindata.org/terrorism)
* [Homicides](https://ourworldindata.org/homicides)

# Key Insights on War and Peace[](#key-insights)

Some conflicts are much, much deadlier than most

Conflict deaths have declined; it is on us that this trend continues

Armed conflict is a rare cause of death in most years and countries

Some countries are much more affected by conflict than others

Armed conflict is common and takes different forms

Relationships between countries have become more peaceful

#### Some conflicts are much, much deadlier than most

There are very large differences in how deadly different wars are: most death tolls are relatively small, a few are large, and very few are extremely large.

The chart shows this for all conventional wars between 1800 and 2011, relying on data from Project Mars.[2](#note-2)

Even though most wars killed several thousand people, we can barely make them out in the chart.[3](#note-3)

This is because the big wars were _much_ more deadly: wars like the Russian Civil War and the Korean War killed several hundred thousand people. And wars such as the Chinese Civil War and the Vietnam War killed between 1 and 2 million combatants.

But the deaths in the World Wars loom even over them: in World War I, more than 7 million soldiers died.

And in World War II alone, more than 21 million combatants died.

Three-quarters of all war deaths since 1800 happened in just these two wars, and 90% in the biggest ten wars; this is one of the reasons why we have to treat any [trends over time](https://ourworldindata.org/war-and-peace?insight=conflict-deaths-have-declined-it-is-on-us-that-this-trend-continues#key-insights) with caution.

![Beeswarm plot in landscape format showing that most combatants in conventional wars over the last two hundred years have died in a few, very deadly conflicts.](https://ourworldindata.org/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/qLq-8BTgXU8yG0N6HnOy8g/0e2122c1-26f1-4ea1-e57f-2968e21ca100/w=4096)

Download

#### Conflict deaths have declined; it is on us that this trend continues

Fewer people died in conflicts in recent decades than in most of the 20th century.

The chart shows that several million people died in conflicts in the years after World War II.

After falling to much lower levels in the 1950s, conflict deaths surged again in the 1970s and 1980s. But this time, they peaked at 300,000 deaths annually.

They fell to much lower levels in the 1990s and have stayed below previous peaks in the decades since.

We see these lower numbers of deaths also in other [data](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/deaths-in-wars?time=1946..latest) [sources](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/deaths-in-interstate-conflicts-gibler-miller?time=1946..latest).

But there are several reasons we cannot be confident that this decline in conflict deaths will continue.

First, the chart shows more deaths in the last decade and, most recently, a spike in deaths due to wars [in Ethiopia and Ukraine](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/deaths-in-armed-conflicts?tab=chart&country=ETH~UKR). The trends also differ [by world region](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/deaths-in-state-based-conflicts-by-region?facet=entity&uniformYAxis=0): deaths have plummeted and stayed low for Asia and Oceania, but they have recently increased in the Middle East and soared in Africa and Europe.

One more reason we cannot be confident is that the deadliness of conflicts shows a lot of variation from year to year. [Some wars are much deadlier than others](https://ourworldindata.org/war-and-peace?insight=some-conflicts-are-much-much-deadlier-than-most#key-insights), so a single deadly conflict could change this trend completely. Researchers have used statistical tests to tell actual trends from random fluctuations but have come to different conclusions.[4](#note-4)

But the absence of a clear trend should not cause despair: countries have built [more peaceful relations](https://ourworldindata.org/war-and-peace?insight=relationships-between-countries-have-become-more-peaceful#key-insights) between and within them. It is up to us that these historical trends continue over the next decades and centuries.

##### What you should know about this data

* There are several other leading approaches to measuring conflicts. You can explore them in our [Conflict Data Explorer](https://ourworldindata.org/explorers/conflict-data).

![](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/deaths-in-state-based-conflicts-by-region.png)

#### Armed conflict is a rare cause of death in most years and countries

Globally, close to 80,000 people died due to fighting in armed conflicts in 2019.

This means conflicts caused around 1 in 700 deaths.

This is shown in the chart, which presents what people died from during that year. You can find conflict deaths in the bottom-right corner.

Armed conflict is a much rarer cause of death than non-communicable (in blue) or infectious diseases (in red). It is also less common than other causes of _violent_ death: more than five times as many people died from homicides in 2019, and almost ten times as many from suicide.

Yet, the [number of conflict deaths](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/deaths-in-armed-conflicts-by-type) can change a lot from year to year — in 2005, fewer than 20,000 people died in armed conflicts, while in 1994, in the wake of the genocide in Rwanda, it was more than 800,000\. During the two World Wars, armed conflict was a leading cause of death, with [several million deaths per year](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/deaths-in-wars).

And while armed conflict is a rare cause of death globally in most years, it is much [more common in some countries](https://ourworldindata.org/war-and-peace?insight=some-countries-are-much-more-affected-by-conflict-than-others#key-insights).

##### What you should know about this data

* For its data on conflict and terrorism deaths, the data source — the Global Burden of Disease study by the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME) — relies on several major sources, including UCDP[5](#note-5) and the Peace Research Institute Oslo (PRIO).[6](#note-6)
* We separated terrorism deaths from conflict deaths by using data from the Global Terrorism Database.[7](#note-7)

![Tree map of causes of death globally in 2019, with non-communicable diseases in blue, communicable or infectious diseases in red, and injuries in green. The most common causes of deaths are non-communicable diseases such as heart diseases and cancers, while injuries and especially deaths from violence are rare. This version says 'conflict' instead of 'war' deaths, staying closer to IHME's terminology.](https://ourworldindata.org/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/qLq-8BTgXU8yG0N6HnOy8g/9fccd3e0-d831-49b3-b485-3eda86a44900/w=3086)

Download

#### Some countries are much more affected by conflict than others

There are very large differences in the number of deaths from conflict across the world.

The map shows annual deaths from armed conflicts in each country.

We see that a large number of countries around the world are relatively peaceful. In them, few to no people die due to conflicts. Many of them are in Europe, but there are countries where few die in conflicts in all world regions.

In other countries, however, deaths from conflict are common. They see dozens, hundreds, or even thousands of deaths per year. In a few, conflict deaths account for [several percent of all deaths](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/share-of-deaths-by-cause?country=~AFG) in a year.

These global differences [look similar](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/death-rate-in-armed-conflicts) when we consider that countries differ in the size of their populations.

The countries with the most conflict deaths can change frequently. In 2022, more than 40% of the people who died from conflict worldwide were in Ethiopia. In 2021, it was Afghanistan, with almost a third of all global conflict deaths occurring there.

The countries with the most conflict deaths also differ depending on whether we look at [interstate](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/deaths-in-interstate-conflicts), [intrastate](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/deaths-in-intrastate-conflicts), [non-state](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/deaths-in-non-state-conflicts) conflicts, or [one-sided violence](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/deaths-from-one-sided-violence).

![](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/deaths-in-armed-conflicts-by-country.png)

#### Armed conflict is common and takes different forms

As the chart shows, at least 150 ongoing armed conflicts have been recorded each year recently. This number is up from previous decades, but even then, it rarely fell below 100, and there has been no year without armed conflict [for centuries](https://ourworldindata.org/explorers/conflict-data?facet=none&country=~OWID%5FWRL&Conflict+type=All+armed+conflicts&Measure=Number&Conflict+sub-type=by+type&Data+source=Conflict+Catalog&Sub-measure=ongoing+conflicts).

Wars — usually defined as armed conflicts that are especially deadly — [have been rarer](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/number-of-wars-project-mars), with between 0 and 12 active wars per year. Still, there have been very few years without any.

The frequency of armed conflicts also differs depending on who fights them.

Armed conflict can occur between states (interstate), between a state and a non-state armed group within its territory (intrastate) or outside of it (extrasystemic), between non-state armed groups (non-state), or between an armed group and civilians (one-sided violence).

Looking at these conflict types more closely, we see that there have been no extrasystemic conflicts in recent decades. They disappeared after decolonization [in the middle of the 20th century](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/number-of-state-based-conflicts).

Interstate conflicts are rare: there have been, at most, three ongoing conflicts of this type in any given year in the last three decades. And several years in that period saw no such conflict at all.

Intrastate conflicts and one-sided violence are more frequent. In recent decades, there have been several dozen conflicts of these types ongoing each year.

And non-state conflicts have become the most common type; they have been the primary driver of the recent increase in conflicts.

##### What you should know about this data

* There are several other leading approaches to measuring conflicts. You can explore them in our [Conflict Data Explorer](https://ourworldindata.org/explorers/conflict-data).

![](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/number-of-armed-conflicts.png)

#### Relationships between countries have become more peaceful

Researchers have argued that we should think of peace as more than just the absence of violence (called _negative_ peace), but envision it as sustained cooperation or even mutual protection between groups (_positive_ peace).[8](#note-8)

The chart shows global data that uses this distinction to classify the bilateral relationships between countries into different levels of peacefulness or hostility, expressed here as the share of each type of relationship.

Most relationships between countries are characterized as negative and positive peace — which is further split into warm peace and security communities.

Only a small percentage of relationships are classified as rivalries. These rivalries are separated into lesser or severe rivalries by the researchers who produced this data.

We also see that relationships between countries have changed over time: more than a century ago, in 1900, most countries did not use violence against each other, but none had highly cooperative relationships. And almost 20% of relationships were rivals that occasionally or frequently used violence against each other.

Conflict surged during the two World Wars and the early years of the Cold War. But then, rivalries steadily declined, and bilateral cooperation spread. Importantly, this happened while [many more countries became independent](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/number-of-countries), and many more pairs of countries [started having a relationship](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/peaceful-and-hostile-relationships-between-states?stackMode=absolute).[9](#note-9)

Many countries deepened their ties in the 1990s and 2000s, predominantly in the European Union. This turned almost a fifth of relationships into security communities.

Recent years have seen slight increases in rivalries and declines in peaceful relationships. But bilateral relations remain much more peaceful than over the entire 20th century.

Even if we are more ambitious in our vision of peace, we see that the world has made progress.

![](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/peaceful-and-hostile-relationships-between-states.png)

description: How common are armed conflict and peace between and within countries? How is this changing over time? Explore research and data on war and peace.
title: War and Peace
image: https://ourworldindata.org/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/qLq-8BTgXU8yG0N6HnOy8g/aa942158-857b-4a7a-76b1-596cc88e3f00/public
---

Since 1800, more than [37 million people](https://ourworldindata.org/war-and-peace?insight=some-conflicts-are-much-much-deadlier-than-most#key-insights) worldwide have died while actively fighting in wars.

The number would be much higher still if it also considered the civilians who died due to the fighting, the increased number of deaths from hunger and disease resulting from these conflicts, and the deaths in smaller conflicts that are not considered wars.[1](#note-1)

Wars are also terrible in many other ways: they make people’s lives insecure, lower their living standards, destroy the environment, and, if fought between countries armed with [nuclear weapons](https://ourworldindata.org/nuclear-weapons), can be an existential threat to humanity.

Looking at the news alone, it can be difficult to understand whether more or less people are dying as a result of war than in the past. One has to rely on statistics that are carefully collected so that they can be compared over time.

While every war is a tragedy, the data suggests that [fewer people died](https://ourworldindata.org/war-and-peace?insight=conflict-deaths-have-declined-it-is-on-us-that-this-trend-continues#key-insights) in conflicts in recent decades than in most of the 20th century. Countries have also built more peaceful relations [between](https://ourworldindata.org/war-and-peace?insight=relationships-between-countries-have-become-more-peaceful#key-insights) and [within](https://ourworldindata.org/democracy) them.

How many wars are avoided, and whether the trend of fewer deaths in them continues, is up to our own actions. Conflict deaths recently increased in the Middle East, Africa, and Europe, stressing that the future of these trends is uncertain.

On this page, you can find data, visualizations, and writing on how common war and peace are between and within countries, and how this has changed over time.

#### Related topics

* [Military Personnel and Spending](https://ourworldindata.org/military-personnel-spending)
* [Nuclear Weapons](https://ourworldindata.org/nuclear-weapons)
* [Terrorism](https://ourworldindata.org/terrorism)
* [Homicides](https://ourworldindata.org/homicides)

# Key Insights on War and Peace[](#key-insights)

Some conflicts are much, much deadlier than most

Conflict deaths have declined; it is on us that this trend continues

Armed conflict is a rare cause of death in most years and countries

Some countries are much more affected by conflict than others

Armed conflict is common and takes different forms

Relationships between countries have become more peaceful

#### Some conflicts are much, much deadlier than most

There are very large differences in how deadly different wars are: most death tolls are relatively small, a few are large, and very few are extremely large.

The chart shows this for all conventional wars between 1800 and 2011, relying on data from Project Mars.[2](#note-2)

Even though most wars killed several thousand people, we can barely make them out in the chart.[3](#note-3)

This is because the big wars were _much_ more deadly: wars like the Russian Civil War and the Korean War killed several hundred thousand people. And wars such as the Chinese Civil War and the Vietnam War killed between 1 and 2 million combatants.

But the deaths in the World Wars loom even over them: in World War I, more than 7 million soldiers died.

And in World War II alone, more than 21 million combatants died.

Three-quarters of all war deaths since 1800 happened in just these two wars, and 90% in the biggest ten wars; this is one of the reasons why we have to treat any [trends over time](https://ourworldindata.org/war-and-peace?insight=conflict-deaths-have-declined-it-is-on-us-that-this-trend-continues#key-insights) with caution.

![Beeswarm plot in landscape format showing that most combatants in conventional wars over the last two hundred years have died in a few, very deadly conflicts.](https://ourworldindata.org/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/qLq-8BTgXU8yG0N6HnOy8g/0e2122c1-26f1-4ea1-e57f-2968e21ca100/w=4096)

Download

#### Conflict deaths have declined; it is on us that this trend continues

Fewer people died in conflicts in recent decades than in most of the 20th century.

The chart shows that several million people died in conflicts in the years after World War II.

After falling to much lower levels in the 1950s, conflict deaths surged again in the 1970s and 1980s. But this time, they peaked at 300,000 deaths annually.

They fell to much lower levels in the 1990s and have stayed below previous peaks in the decades since.

We see these lower numbers of deaths also in other [data](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/deaths-in-wars?time=1946..latest) [sources](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/deaths-in-interstate-conflicts-gibler-miller?time=1946..latest).

But there are several reasons we cannot be confident that this decline in conflict deaths will continue.

First, the chart shows more deaths in the last decade and, most recently, a spike in deaths due to wars [in Ethiopia and Ukraine](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/deaths-in-armed-conflicts?tab=chart&country=ETH~UKR). The trends also differ [by world region](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/deaths-in-state-based-conflicts-by-region?facet=entity&uniformYAxis=0): deaths have plummeted and stayed low for Asia and Oceania, but they have recently increased in the Middle East and soared in Africa and Europe.

One more reason we cannot be confident is that the deadliness of conflicts shows a lot of variation from year to year. [Some wars are much deadlier than others](https://ourworldindata.org/war-and-peace?insight=some-conflicts-are-much-much-deadlier-than-most#key-insights), so a single deadly conflict could change this trend completely. Researchers have used statistical tests to tell actual trends from random fluctuations but have come to different conclusions.[4](#note-4)

But the absence of a clear trend should not cause despair: countries have built [more peaceful relations](https://ourworldindata.org/war-and-peace?insight=relationships-between-countries-have-become-more-peaceful#key-insights) between and within them. It is up to us that these historical trends continue over the next decades and centuries.

##### What you should know about this data

* There are several other leading approaches to measuring conflicts. You can explore them in our [Conflict Data Explorer](https://ourworldindata.org/explorers/conflict-data).

![](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/deaths-in-state-based-conflicts-by-region.png)

#### Armed conflict is a rare cause of death in most years and countries

Globally, close to 80,000 people died due to fighting in armed conflicts in 2019.

This means conflicts caused around 1 in 700 deaths.

This is shown in the chart, which presents what people died from during that year. You can find conflict deaths in the bottom-right corner.

Armed conflict is a much rarer cause of death than non-communicable (in blue) or infectious diseases (in red). It is also less common than other causes of _violent_ death: more than five times as many people died from homicides in 2019, and almost ten times as many from suicide.

Yet, the [number of conflict deaths](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/deaths-in-armed-conflicts-by-type) can change a lot from year to year — in 2005, fewer than 20,000 people died in armed conflicts, while in 1994, in the wake of the genocide in Rwanda, it was more than 800,000\. During the two World Wars, armed conflict was a leading cause of death, with [several million deaths per year](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/deaths-in-wars).

And while armed conflict is a rare cause of death globally in most years, it is much [more common in some countries](https://ourworldindata.org/war-and-peace?insight=some-countries-are-much-more-affected-by-conflict-than-others#key-insights).

##### What you should know about this data

* For its data on conflict and terrorism deaths, the data source — the Global Burden of Disease study by the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME) — relies on several major sources, including UCDP[5](#note-5) and the Peace Research Institute Oslo (PRIO).[6](#note-6)
* We separated terrorism deaths from conflict deaths by using data from the Global Terrorism Database.[7](#note-7)

![Tree map of causes of death globally in 2019, with non-communicable diseases in blue, communicable or infectious diseases in red, and injuries in green. The most common causes of deaths are non-communicable diseases such as heart diseases and cancers, while injuries and especially deaths from violence are rare. This version says 'conflict' instead of 'war' deaths, staying closer to IHME's terminology.](https://ourworldindata.org/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/qLq-8BTgXU8yG0N6HnOy8g/9fccd3e0-d831-49b3-b485-3eda86a44900/w=3086)

Download

#### Some countries are much more affected by conflict than others

There are very large differences in the number of deaths from conflict across the world.

The map shows annual deaths from armed conflicts in each country.

We see that a large number of countries around the world are relatively peaceful. In them, few to no people die due to conflicts. Many of them are in Europe, but there are countries where few die in conflicts in all world regions.

In other countries, however, deaths from conflict are common. They see dozens, hundreds, or even thousands of deaths per year. In a few, conflict deaths account for [several percent of all deaths](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/share-of-deaths-by-cause?country=~AFG) in a year.

These global differences [look similar](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/death-rate-in-armed-conflicts) when we consider that countries differ in the size of their populations.

The countries with the most conflict deaths can change frequently. In 2022, more than 40% of the people who died from conflict worldwide were in Ethiopia. In 2021, it was Afghanistan, with almost a third of all global conflict deaths occurring there.

The countries with the most conflict deaths also differ depending on whether we look at [interstate](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/deaths-in-interstate-conflicts), [intrastate](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/deaths-in-intrastate-conflicts), [non-state](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/deaths-in-non-state-conflicts) conflicts, or [one-sided violence](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/deaths-from-one-sided-violence).

![](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/deaths-in-armed-conflicts-by-country.png)

#### Armed conflict is common and takes different forms

As the chart shows, at least 150 ongoing armed conflicts have been recorded each year recently. This number is up from previous decades, but even then, it rarely fell below 100, and there has been no year without armed conflict [for centuries](https://ourworldindata.org/explorers/conflict-data?facet=none&country=~OWID%5FWRL&Conflict+type=All+armed+conflicts&Measure=Number&Conflict+sub-type=by+type&Data+source=Conflict+Catalog&Sub-measure=ongoing+conflicts).

Wars — usually defined as armed conflicts that are especially deadly — [have been rarer](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/number-of-wars-project-mars), with between 0 and 12 active wars per year. Still, there have been very few years without any.

The frequency of armed conflicts also differs depending on who fights them.

Armed conflict can occur between states (interstate), between a state and a non-state armed group within its territory (intrastate) or outside of it (extrasystemic), between non-state armed groups (non-state), or between an armed group and civilians (one-sided violence).

Looking at these conflict types more closely, we see that there have been no extrasystemic conflicts in recent decades. They disappeared after decolonization [in the middle of the 20th century](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/number-of-state-based-conflicts).

Interstate conflicts are rare: there have been, at most, three ongoing conflicts of this type in any given year in the last three decades. And several years in that period saw no such conflict at all.

Intrastate conflicts and one-sided violence are more frequent. In recent decades, there have been several dozen conflicts of these types ongoing each year.

And non-state conflicts have become the most common type; they have been the primary driver of the recent increase in conflicts.

##### What you should know about this data

* There are several other leading approaches to measuring conflicts. You can explore them in our [Conflict Data Explorer](https://ourworldindata.org/explorers/conflict-data).

![](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/number-of-armed-conflicts.png)

#### Relationships between countries have become more peaceful

Researchers have argued that we should think of peace as more than just the absence of violence (called _negative_ peace), but envision it as sustained cooperation or even mutual protection between groups (_positive_ peace).[8](#note-8)

The chart shows global data that uses this distinction to classify the bilateral relationships between countries into different levels of peacefulness or hostility, expressed here as the share of each type of relationship.

Most relationships between countries are characterized as negative and positive peace — which is further split into warm peace and security communities.

Only a small percentage of relationships are classified as rivalries. These rivalries are separated into lesser or severe rivalries by the researchers who produced this data.

We also see that relationships between countries have changed over time: more than a century ago, in 1900, most countries did not use violence against each other, but none had highly cooperative relationships. And almost 20% of relationships were rivals that occasionally or frequently used violence against each other.

Conflict surged during the two World Wars and the early years of the Cold War. But then, rivalries steadily declined, and bilateral cooperation spread. Importantly, this happened while [many more countries became independent](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/number-of-countries), and many more pairs of countries [started having a relationship](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/peaceful-and-hostile-relationships-between-states?stackMode=absolute).[9](#note-9)

Many countries deepened their ties in the 1990s and 2000s, predominantly in the European Union. This turned almost a fifth of relationships into security communities.

Recent years have seen slight increases in rivalries and declines in peaceful relationships. But bilateral relations remain much more peaceful than over the entire 20th century.

Even if we are more ambitious in our vision of peace, we see that the world has made progress.

![](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/peaceful-and-hostile-relationships-between-states.png)

content.thinking:
This data is by region and year, but doesn't show individual wars. Let me search for a more specific dataset or visualization that shows individual interstate wars by death toll. The Project Mars data should have this, but it seems to be all wars including civil wars. 

Let me look at the data more carefully. From the original CSV I fetched, I need to identify which wars are interstate (between states) rather than civil wars (intrastate) or other types.

Looking at the data from the wars ranked by death toll:
- World War II: 21,058,660 - definitely interstate
- World War I: 7,107,951 - definitely interstate
- Second Sino-Japanese War: 1,689,000 - interstate (between China and Japan)
- Vietnam War: 1,062,068 - complex classification, but the Project Mars data classifies it
- Chinese Civil War: 1,200,000 - civil war (NOT interstate)
- Korean War: 543,936 - interstate (North Korea/China vs South Korea/UN)
- Napoleonic Wars: 570,328 - interstate
- Russian Civil War: 379,483 - civil war (NOT interstate)
- Spanish Civil War: 203,839 - civil war (NOT interstate)
- Iran-Iraq War: 228,220 - interstate

Let me search for more specific information about Project Mars classification of interstate wars.

content.text: Let me search for specific information about the top interstate wars:

description: There are many ways to measure armed conflicts and conflict deaths. What approaches do different researchers take? And when is which approach best?
title: How major sources collect data on conflicts and conflict deaths, and when to use which one
image: https://ourworldindata.org/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/qLq-8BTgXU8yG0N6HnOy8g/485c0cd1-6f9e-4a7c-655a-fe65fa554800/public
---

[Home](https://ourworldindata.org/)[War & Peace](https://ourworldindata.org/war-and-peace)

#### More on conflict data

Explore the data discussed in this article in our work on [War and Peace](https://ourworldindata.org/war-and-peace) and our [Conflict Data Explorers](https://ourworldindata.org/war-and-peace-data-explorers), and read more about its measures in [our article on them](https://ourworldindata.org/conflict-measures-how-do-researchers-measure-how-common-and-deadly-armed-conflicts-are).

Measuring armed conflicts and conflict deaths across the world helps us understand how people’s lives and livelihoods are affected by large-scale violence.

But this comes with many challenges. People do not always agree on what characteristics define an armed conflict. Even once defined, these characteristics — especially how many people died in them — are difficult to assess.

The people affected are not always asked who has died around them due to the conflict.

The conflict parties may underreport deaths to claim success, or overreport them to encourage intervention by third parties.

Independent observers may also struggle to be present in all places and document a conflict’s death toll.

So how do researchers address these challenges?

In our work on [War and Peace](https://ourworldindata.org/war-and-peace), we provide data from six sources that identify armed conflicts and count their deaths:

* Uppsala Conflict Data Program (UCDP)[1](#note-1)
* Project Mars by Jason Lyall (2022)[2](#note-2)
* Militarized Interstate Events by Douglas Gibler and Steven Miller[3](#note-3)
* Correlates of War (CoW)[4](#note-4)
* Peace Research Institute Oslo (PRIO)[5](#note-5)
* Conflict Catalog by Peter Brecke (1999)[6](#note-6)

These sources all measure armed conflicts and their deaths; they cover many countries and years, and researchers and policymakers frequently use them.

In our [Conflict Data Explorers](https://ourworldindata.org/war-and-peace-data-explorers), you can delve into global and regional overviews of conflicts and their deaths.

Reassuringly, sources typically agree about big differences in the deaths from armed conflicts: they readily distinguish between deadly and peaceful years.

But they do not always agree. They often come to different assessments about _how_ widespread and deadly some years were.

Why do these sources arrive at different numbers? And is there any best approach?

I summarize the key similarities and differences between the different approaches in this article and when to use which one.

# What conflicts are covered?[](#what-conflicts-are-covered)

In this table and the ones that follow, I summarize what armed conflicts and conflict deaths each data source covers.[7](#note-7)

| UCDP                                                | Armed conflicts: interstate, intrastate, extrastate, non-state, and one-sided violenceAt least 25 deaths during a year (based on most plausible estimate)[8](#note-8)                                  |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Project Mars                                        | Conventional wars: interstate; de facto also intrastate and extrastateAt least 500 deaths (based on highest plausible estimate)Primary combatants have differentiated militaries, and clear frontlines |
| Militarized Interstate Events                       | Militarized interstate confrontations: interstate threats of force, display of force, use of force, war                                                                                                |
| Correlates of War — Wars                            | Wars: interstate, intrastate, extrastate, and non-stateAt least 1,000 deaths during a year                                                                                                             |
| Correlates of War — Militarized Interstate Disputes | Militarized interstate disputes: interstate threats of force, display of force, use of force, warAt least use of force threatenedAt least 1,000 deaths during a year for war                           |
| Peace Research Institute Oslo                       | Armed conflicts: interstate, intrastate, and extrastateAt least 25 deaths during a year                                                                                                                |
| Conflict Catalog                                    | Violent political conflicts: interstate, intrastate, extrastate, non-state and one-sided violenceAt least 32 deaths during a year                                                                      |

All sources characterize an armed conflict as a disagreement between organized groups that involves force. For most datasets, this means that force is used. But for the Militarized Interstate Events data and Correlates of War’s Militarized Interstate Disputes data, this can also mean that force is threatened or displayed.

Approaches also differ in what types of conflicts they cover and how many deaths they must cause to be included.

They all include armed conflicts where the primary combatants are states (interstate conflicts), and most cover those conflicts between a state and an armed group that is not a state inside the state’s territory (intrastate conflicts) or outside the state’s territory (extrastate conflicts).[9](#note-9) These conflicts are sometimes grouped together as “state-based” conflicts.

Some approaches go further and also include conflicts where neither armed group is a state (non-state conflicts). [10](#note-10) And some even include violence by an armed group — state or non-state — against civilians (one-sided violence).

Most sources only include conflicts if they cause many deaths. Some set a threshold of at least 500 or 1,000 annual or total deaths, and then call these deadly conflicts _wars_. Others include more minor armed conflicts that cause a few dozen deaths during a year. And the Militarized Interstate Events data and Correlates of War’s Militarized Interstate Disputes data also include conflicts in which no one died.

Finally, the specific definitions of the sources mean that their conflicts differ slightly beyond their differences in conflict type and death toll. The biggest of these minor differences is that Project Mars only includes conventional wars, those fought between differentiated militaries along clear frontlines. Others do not make such a distinction.

# Which deaths are included?[](#which-deaths-are-included)

The data sources also differ in who they include in their death counts and how they were killed.

| UCDP                                                | Total, combatant, and civilian deaths, due to fighting                          |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Project Mars                                        | Deaths of combatants, due to fighting                                           |
| Militarized Interstate Events                       | Deaths of combatants, due to fighting                                           |
| Correlates of War — War Data                        | Deaths of combatants, due to fighting, disease, and starvation                  |
| Correlates of War — Militarized Interstate Disputes | Deaths of combatants, due to fighting                                           |
| Peace Research Institute Oslo                       | Deaths of combatants and civilians, due to fighting                             |
| Conflict Catalog                                    | Total, combatant, and civilian deaths, due to fighting, disease, and starvation |

All sources record deaths, the people killed in the conflict. This is different from other sources which record casualties, which include both deaths and those wounded. Yet other sources even tally losses, including both casualties and those deserted.[11](#note-11)

But some approaches only include deaths of combatants — those doing the fighting. Others also include civilians — those who do not take up any weapons but may be killed accidentally or intentionally (in cases of one-sided violence).

These civilian deaths also include victims of terrorist attacks, as long as the attack was carried out by an armed group.[12](#note-12)

And some approaches only include direct, or battle-related, deaths — those due to the fighting. Meanwhile, others include direct and indirect, or war-related, deaths — both those due to fighting, and those due to disease or starvation caused by the conflict.

# What years and countries are covered?[](#what-years-and-countries-are-covered)

All data sources provide historical data and cover conflicts worldwide. But they differ in what years they cover, and which countries and regions they consider sovereign states.

| UCDP                                                | 1989 — ongoingGlobal                                                                                     |
| --------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Project Mars                                        | 1800 — 2011 / ongoingGlobal                                                                              |
| Militarized Interstate Events                       | 1816 — 2014 / ongoingGlobal                                                                              |
| Correlates of War — War Data                        | 1816 — 2007 (extrastate, non-state), 1816 — 2010 (inter-state), 1816 — 2014 (intrastate) / ongoingGlobal |
| Correlates of War — Militarized Interstate Disputes | 1816 — 2014 / ongoingGlobal                                                                              |
| Peace Research Institute Oslo                       | 1946 — 2008Global                                                                                        |
| Conflict Catalog                                    | 1400 — 2000Global                                                                                        |

UCDP currently provides the most recent data, as it is updated each year. Other sources are updated less frequently and currently have a delay of about a decade on their most recent data (Project Mars, Militarized Interstate Events, and Correlates of War), or they are no longer maintained and will likely not be updated for recent decades (Conflict Catalog and PRIO).

In turn, UCDP only begins at the end of the Cold War. In contrast, the other sources start in the mid- or early 20th century (PRIO), the early 19th century (Project Mars, Militarized Interstate Events, and Correlates of War), or even reach as far back in time as the year 1400 (Conflict Catalog).

The data sources also differ in which countries and regions they consider sovereign states. Correlates of War and Militarized Interstate Events use the state system by [Correlates of War](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/sovereign-state-cow), which until 1919 requires diplomatic recognition by France and the United Kingdom for a country to be included.

UCDP and PRIO meanwhile use the slightly more inclusive list of sovereign states by [Gleditsch and Ward](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/sovereign-state-gleditsch-ward). Project Mars and the Conflict Catalog have even more expansive definitions of statehood, and are closer to the state system as identified by [Butcher and Griffiths](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/sovereign-state-butcher-griffiths).

This affects how some conflicts are classified, as an extrastate or non-state war in Correlates of War’s war data can be classified as an interstate or civil war in Project Mars. And it affects how conflict rates are [calculated](https://ourworldindata.org/conflict-measures-how-do-researchers-measure-how-common-and-deadly-armed-conflicts-are), as the number of countries for each year can [differ a lot](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/number-of-countries), [especially](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/number-of-countries-by-region) for Africa and Asia and Oceania.

# How are conflicts and deaths identified?[](#how-are-conflicts-and-deaths-identified)

Generally, the data sources are similar in how they go about assessing conflicts and the deaths in them.

| UCDP                                                | Evaluations by own researchers of news reports, other contemporary sources, and academic research                                                                |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Project Mars                                        | Evaluations by own researchers of academic research (including UCDP and CoW), news reports, and other contemporary sources                                       |
| Militarized Interstate Events                       | Evaluations by own researchers of academic research (including CoW) and news reports, other contemporary sources, and academic research                          |
| Correlates of War — War Data                        | Evaluations by own researchers of academic research                                                                                                              |
| Correlates of War — Militarized Interstate Disputes | Evaluations by own researchers of academic research and news reports filtered by machine learning                                                                |
| Peace Research Institute Oslo                       | Evaluations by own researchers of academic research (including UCDP), official death statistics, surveys, news reports, and other archival sources[13](#note-13) |
| Conflict Catalog                                    | Own evaluations of academic research (including CoW) and other sources                                                                                           |

All rely on researchers evaluating independent news reports, academic research, or both. Some also supplement these primary sources with available surveys of the affected populations, or official death statistics.

The primary sources they use can partially overlap. Some use the same sources, such as the encyclopedias by Micheal Clodfelter[14](#note-14) Lewis Fry Richardson[15](#note-15), and Pitirim Sorokin[16](#note-16). Or they outright rely on each other as the sources: PRIO and Project Mars use UCDP data, and Project Mars, Militarized Interstate Events, and the Conflict Catalog build on Correlates of War.[17](#note-17)

# How do sources work to measure what they want to measure?[](#how-do-sources-work-to-measure-what-they-want-to-measure)

The next tables summarize how the data sources address the specific challenges of measuring armed conflicts and conflict deaths. The first challenge is to make their assessments valid — to actually measure what they want to measure.

| UCDP                                                | Own researchers know measurement procedures and conflicts wellInclude civilian deaths, as difference to combatants can be blurryExclude deaths due to disease and starvation as well as wounded, as difficult to identify                                                                        |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Project Mars                                        | Own researchers know measurement procedures wellExclude civilian deaths, deaths due to disease and starvation, as well as wounded, as interested in military lethality on the battlefield                                                                                                        |
| Militarized Interstate Events                       | Own researchers know measurement procedures wellInvestigate closely country-pairs with high predicted likelihood of conflict                                                                                                                                                                     |
| Correlates of War — War Data                        | Own researchers know measurement procedures wellInclude deaths due to disease and starvation, as they are integral to war, and often not distinguished from fighting in sourcesExclude civilian deaths, as difficult to identifySometimes estimate deaths if only number of casualties available |
| Correlates of War — Militarized Interstate Disputes | Own researchers know measurement procedures wellMachine learning can process vast numbers of news reportsGroup deaths into broad ranges because number of deaths often uncertain                                                                                                                 |
| Peace Research Institute Oslo                       | Own researchers know measurement procedures wellInclude civilian deaths, as difference to combatants can be blurryExclude deaths due to disease and starvation, as difficult to identify                                                                                                         |
| Conflict Catalog                                    | Own researchers know measurement procedures well                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |

In general, the sources relying on their own researchers have the advantage that these researchers know the respective definitions of armed conflicts and related deaths well and are very familiar with the measurement procedures, which makes it more likely that they code as intended.

However, the sources differ in the deaths they include because they weigh the challenges of measurement differently. Some include civilian deaths because they often find it too difficult to distinguish them from combatant deaths.

Others exclude them because they find them too difficult to identify comprehensively or because they are only interested in the actions of militaries on the battlefield.

Some approaches include deaths due to disease and starvation because they consider them a fundamental part of war, and because primary sources often do not distinguish between them and deaths due to fighting. But others do not, as they find such indirect deaths too challenging to identify comprehensively.

Finally, Correlates of War’s war data sometimes estimates the number of deaths based on the number of conflict casualties, if only those are available. And its Militarized Interstate Disputes data mostly groups deaths into broad ranges, as it finds determining more specific numbers too uncertain.

# How do sources work to make assessments precise?[](#how-do-sources-work-to-make-assessments-precise)

The sources are also concerned with making their assessments precise and reliable.

| UCDP                                                | Many and different types of sources usedNot covering earlier yearsConflicts disaggregated into years and individual events (with at least one death per event)Report types of deaths separately |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Project Mars                                        | More than 100 researchers split into adversarial teams search at least 10 quality sources per deaths estimateNot covering earlier yearsBig and recurrent wars disaggregated into campaigns      |
| Militarized Interstate Events                       | Many and different types of primary sources usedNot covering earlier yearsConflicts disaggregated into years and individual events                                                              |
| Correlates of War — War Data                        | Many and different types of primary sources usedNot covering earlier years                                                                                                                      |
| Correlates of War — Militarized Interstate Disputes | Many and different types of primary sources usedNot covering earlier yearsConflicts partially disaggregated into individual incidents                                                           |
| Peace Research Institute Oslo                       | Many and different types of sources usedNot covering earlier yearsConflicts disaggregated into years                                                                                            |
| Conflict Catalog                                    | Many and different types of primary sources usedNot covering earlier yearsBig conflicts disaggregated into smaller onesReport types of deaths separately                                        |

They all use many primary sources, and most use different types of sources, such as news reports, academic books and articles, or NGO documents.

They also all avoid covering conflicts that happened even earlier — even though they differ in how far they think they can go back in time and still have data that is sufficiently reliable: UCDP begins in 1989, whereas the Conflict Catalog starts in the year 1400.[18](#note-18)

Several sources also disaggregate their data to make it more precise: they split their estimates of deaths into total, combatant, and civilian deaths, when possible; disaggregate bigger conflicts into smaller ones; or each conflict into years, campaigns, or even specific events.

# How do sources work to make assessments comparable?[](#how-do-sources-work-to-make-assessments-comparable)

The sources also face the challenge of making the data comparable across conflicts and time.

| UCDP                                                | Researchers have very precise definitions of conflict, deaths, and other event characteristicsGlobal news used first, then (sometimes translated) local and specialized sources |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Project Mars                                        | Researchers have very precise definitions of conflict and deathsPrimary sources in 21 languages used                                                                            |
| Militarized Interstate Events                       | Exclude civilian deaths, as they have become more commonGlobal news used because more comprehensive                                                                             |
| Correlates of War — War Data                        | Exclude civilian deaths, as they have become more common                                                                                                                        |
| Correlates of War — Militarized Interstate Disputes | Exclude civilian deaths, as they have become more commonGlobal news used because more comprehensive                                                                             |
| Peace Research Institute Oslo                       | Researchers have precise definitions of conflict and deaths                                                                                                                     |
| Conflict Catalog                                    | Also non-English sources used                                                                                                                                                   |

Some do so by providing their researchers with precise definitions of conflicts and deaths, making it easier to decide which to include.

And some also use primary sources in different languages or first identify conflicts and deaths with global sources and then use more local ones. Others, meanwhile, prefer global sources for their more comprehensive coverage of international affairs.

# How are the remaining differences between primary sources dealt with?[](#how-are-the-remaining-differences-between-primary-sources-dealt-with)

The sources work to address any remaining differences between primary sources, even if they do so differently.

| UCDP                                                | Consider quality of primary sources, discuss within team, use most reliable oneProvide best, low, and high deaths estimates provided if several plausibleUse lower as the best estimate if no primary source is more reliable than others; best estimate therefore likely no overcount |
| --------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Project Mars                                        | Consider quality of primary sources, discuss among coder teamsProvide low and high estimates                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| Militarized Interstate Events                       | Consider quality of primary sources, discuss among codersProvide low and high estimates                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| Correlates of War — War Data                        | Consider quality of primary sources and context (army size, weapons, medical technology, etc.)                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| Correlates of War — Militarized Interstate Disputes | Consider quality of primary sources, discuss among codersProvide low and high estimatesInclude accusations by targeted state even if denied by allegedly targeting state                                                                                                               |
| Peace Research Institute Oslo                       | Consider quality of primary sources, use most reliable oneProvide best, low, and high deaths estimates                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| Conflict Catalog                                    | Consider quality of primary sources                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |

They all consider the quality of primary sources and prefer more reliable ones. Some also consider the context of the conflicts — such as army size and weapons used — to assess which accounts are more plausible.

Others also discuss any discrepancies between researchers on their team. This adds an additional step to make the assessments comparable across coders, conflicts, and time.

Correlates of War’s Militarized Interstate Disputes data partially reconciles differences between conflict parties by erring on the side of including accusations by a targeted state even if the state allegedly targeting it denies them.

Several approaches provide more than one estimate of conflict deaths and share a low, high, and sometimes also a best estimate. By doing so, they avoid forcing themselves to eliminate all uncertainty and possibly biasing their estimates.

UCDP combines these strategies and uses the lower estimate as the best one if no primary source is more reliable than others. It thereby reduces the risk that the estimate overcounts deaths.

# How do sources work to make data accessible and transparent?[](#how-do-sources-work-to-make-data-accessible-and-transparent)

Finally, the data sources all make their data accessible and the underlying measurement transparent. They all publicly release their data, and most make it straightforward to download and use.

| UCDP                                                | Very detailed coding procedures are available and easy to accessJustifies conflict and death characteristicsProvides primary source(s) for each eventProvides context with conflict narratives |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Project Mars                                        | Very detailed coding procedures are available and easy to accessJustifies conflict and death characteristics                                                                                   |
| Militarized Interstate Events                       | Detailed coding procedures are available and easy to accessJustifies conflict and deaths characteristicsProvides context with conflict narratives                                              |
| Correlates of War — War Data                        | Coding procedures are available and partially easy to accessJustifies conflict and death characteristicsProvides context with conflict narratives                                              |
| Correlates of War — Militarized Interstate Disputes | Very detailed coding procedures are available and partially easy to accessJustifies conflict and deaths characteristicsPartially provides context with conflict narratives                     |
| Peace Research Institute Oslo                       | Detailed coding procedures are available and easy to accessJustifies conflict and death characteristics                                                                                        |
| Conflict Catalog                                    | Coding procedures are available and easy to access                                                                                                                                             |

All release descriptions of how they characterize conflicts and deaths and share at least some of the coding procedures guiding the researchers.

Militarized Interstate Events and Correlates of War also provide additional helpful information by describing conflicts in accompanying reports. And UCDP shares the primary sources for each event underlying every conflict.[19](#note-19)

# The best source depends on your questions[](#the-best-source-depends-on-your-questions)

There is no single ‘best’ approach to measuring armed conflicts and their deaths. All sources put a lot of effort into measuring conflicts and deaths in ways that are useful to researchers, policymakers, and interested citizens.

The most appropriate source depends on what questions you want to answer. It is the one that captures the conflicts, deaths, and time you are interested in.

If you are interested in both big and smaller conflicts in recent years, in combatant and civilian deaths, or also non-state conflicts and acts of one-sided violence, UCDP is best.

If you are less interested in the most recent years and more in big and smaller conflicts that involve at least one state in the decades since World War II, PRIO data is best. If you also want the most recent years, you can use our combined UCDP+PRIO data.[20](#note-20)

If you want to study long-term differences and changes over the last two hundred years and it is sufficient to focus on bigger conflicts, then Project Mars is best.

If you are especially interested in specific types of large conflicts over recent centuries, the Correlates of War data is best.

If, instead, you want to explore both big and small conflicts between _states_, the Militarized Interstate Events data is best.

If you want to explore the source that was researchers’ go-to for interstate conflicts for a long time and are fine with its less precise data, Correlates of War’s Militarized Interstate Disputes data is best.

And if you want to study bigger conflicts over more than the last half millennium and are willing to accept lower data quality, the Conflict Catalog is best.

Even if you have a preferred source, it can still be useful to see what other sources show and where they agree and differ.

This means that having several approaches to measuring conflict deaths is not a flaw but a strength: it gives us different tools to understand the past, current state, and possible future of armed conflict around the world.

If you want to explore and compare the data that each dataset produces, you can do so in our work on [War and Peace](https://ourworldindata.org/war-and-peace) and in our [Conflict Data Explorers](https://ourworldindata.org/war-and-peace-data-explorers).

title: How major sources collect data on conflicts and conflict deaths, and when to use which one
image: https://ourworldindata.org/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/qLq-8BTgXU8yG0N6HnOy8g/485c0cd1-6f9e-4a7c-655a-fe65fa554800/public
